definition: Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF or NNMF), also non-negative matrix approximation is a group of algorithms in multivariate analysis and linear algebra where a matrix V is factorized into (usually) two matrices W and H, with the property that all three matrices have no negative elements.
details: This non-negativity makes the resulting matrices easier to inspect. Also, in applications such as processing of audio spectrograms or muscular activity, non-negativity is inherent to the data being considered. Since the problem is not exactly solvable in general, it is commonly approximated numerically. NMF finds applications in such fields as astronomy, computer vision, document clustering, missing data imputation, chemometrics, audio signal processing, recommender systems, and bioinformatics.

explainer.lead: NMF factorizes a matrix V into two matrices W and H, all with no negative entries. It matters because non-negativity matches data like audio spectrograms or muscle activity, and makes the factors easier to inspect.

tiers.eli5: It is like breaking a collection of recipes into a small set of basic ingredients plus how much of each ingredient every recipe uses, with no negative amounts allowed.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers factorize spectrograms or term-document matrices to get parts-based components, but the problem has no exact general solution, so numerical approximation is required. Pitfall: the number of components is chosen by hand, and poor choices give either mushy or overfit decompositions.
tiers.paperLevel: Given V with no negative entries, find W and H, also non-negative, approximately minimizing the reconstruction error between V and WH. Known limits: the factorization is not unique in general and is usually solved heuristically.

explainer.example: Factoring an audio spectrogram into non-negative components yields basis spectra and activations that separate distinct sound sources.
